name: Castor oil on brows/lashes

lead: Castor oil is a thick plant oil pressed from castor beans, made mostly of triglycerides with ricinoleic acid as the main fatty acid. People brush it onto brows and lashes as a folk remedy for thicker, longer hair, and it is popular online.

Forum users report both positive and underwhelming results. Proponents attribute effects to ricinoleic acid and the oil's conditioning; no clinical study of the practice on brows or lashes was identified.

paras: A small amount is brushed onto the brows or the lash base, often at night with a clean spoolie or applicator, over weeks. It is commonly used alongside other brow and lash routines.
Topical use is generally described as low risk, but eye-area products can irritate, and the oil should be kept out of the eyes.

chain: Oil brushed on brows and lashes
Hair believed to thicken or lengthen
angle.text: Practitioners brush castor oil onto brows and lashes as a folk remedy for thicker, longer hair that frames the eyes. Proponents credit its ricinoleic acid and conditioning effect, and it is popular online. Use is driven by user reports rather than trials.

lead: Brushing castor oil onto eyebrows and eyelashes is a long-running home beauty practice used to make brows and lashes look fuller, darker and glossier. Dense lashes and brows frame the eyes, and in looksmaxxing discussion lash and brow density feeds into how the eye area reads, including the impression of canthal tilt.[1] Castor oil is pressed from the seeds of the castor plant and is made up mostly of triglycerides, with ricinoleic acid making up most of its fatty acids.[2][3]

People typically apply a small amount along the lash line or brow with a cotton swab or a spoolie, usually in the evening, and rinse it off the next day.[4] Because the oil is thick and shiny it coats the hair, which many users describe as giving a conditioned, healthier-looking finish; others report that they saw no change in thickness.[4][5] On looksmax.org it is a frequent first suggestion for brows that were shaved or over-tweezed by accident, where members say the hair returns within a few weeks.[5]

No published clinical trial has tested castor oil for brow or lash growth. Healthline's explainer describes the growth claims as anecdotal and notes that a small 2021 randomized trial found castor oil improved eyelid-inflammation symptoms in blepharitis, which is a different outcome.[4] Lash length is largely set by genetics, the number of lash follicles is fixed before birth, and lashes that are pulled out take roughly seven to eight weeks to regrow.[6] Prescription prostaglandin analogs such as bimatoprost are the products documented to lengthen lashes.[6][7][8]
infobox: Castor oil, a ricinoleic acid-rich triglyceride oil from Ricinus communis[2][3]

paras: Castor oil is a pale, viscous vegetable oil with laxative, skin-care and industrial uses.[2] Two forms are sold for beauty use: cold-pressed (clear) and Jamaican black (dark brown), which Healthline describes as sharing the same properties.[4] Roughly 90 percent of the fatty acid content in the oil is ricinolein, the triglyceride of ricinoleic acid, a hydroxylated fatty acid.[3]

Typical online routines apply a small amount to clean, makeup-free lashes or brows in the evening with a cotton swab, taking care to keep it out of the eye, and wash it off in the morning.[4] Healthline's guide also describes patch-testing on the forearm first.[4]

sections.h: Why people want fuller brows and lashes
paras: Brows and lashes shape how the upper face reads. Brow fashion has swung repeatedly: plucked or shaved brows were prized in 8th-century Japan (hikimayu), in the Elizabethan era and in the 1920s and 1930s, while 21st-century fashion has favored fuller, defined brows, including microblading, brow transplants, pencils, powders and dyes.[9] Over-tweezing or shaving is a common reason people look for regrowth help, and Wikipedia notes that people with a history of over-tweezing are considered good candidates for brow transplants.[9]

For lashes, enhancement options include curlers, lifts, tints, mascara, extensions and growth products, and Wikipedia notes that curlers and perms make lashes look longer without lengthening them.[6] Looksmax.org members discuss lashes as part of the eye area, in threads covering lash lifts and tints, trimming or reshaping down-turned lashes, and growth products.[10][11][1] One member's post lamented that a DIY lash lift and tint wearing off left their eyes looking worse.[11] Castor oil sits among the cheapest and easiest of these options, which is part of its appeal.[12]

Castor seeds turn up in Egyptian tombs dating back to about 4000 BC, where the oil mainly fueled lamps, and Greek travelers noted its use for lighting, body ointments and hair care.[13] The Ebers Papyrus, from around 1552 BC, describes it as a laxative, and Cleopatra is said to have used it to brighten the whites of her eyes.[13] Romans applied castor leaves in topical treatments, and castor oil and its derivatives now appear in many cosmetics.[13] Ricinoleic acid was first prepared by Friedrich Krafft in 1888.[3]
The idea of using it specifically for brows and lashes has no single documented originator; it circulates as a folk and beauty-blog remedy and in forum advice.[4][5]

Proponents point to ricinoleic acid and the oil's moisturizing feel. Healthline notes that ricinoleic acid has been discussed as possibly inhibiting prostaglandin D2, a molecule linked to male-pattern baldness, but says this is an unconfirmed possible scalp-hair mechanism that has not been shown to affect eyelashes.[4] Wikipedia's ricinoleic acid page separately lists the compound among agonists of the prostaglandin EP3 receptor, a signaling pathway that is a different one from those targeted by lash-growth drugs.[3]

For context, prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost and bimatoprost are known to lengthen and thicken lashes. A review of prostaglandin-induced hair growth reports that latanoprost, a glaucoma drug, increased lash thickness, length, number and pigmentation, consistent with prolonging the anagen (growth) phase and pushing resting follicles into growth.[7] Bimatoprost was approved in the United States in 2001 and carries a cosmetic eyelash-hypotrichosis indication as Latisse, which Wikipedia reports as prescription-only in the US, EU and Australia.[8] These are separate prescription products, not castor oil.

Lashes have a short growth (anagen) phase compared with scalp hair, which limits how long they grow; in human lashes anagen is short, while scalp hair stays in anagen for years.[14] Wikipedia reports that upper lashes typically measure 7 to 8 mm, that length is almost entirely determined by genetics, that follicles form in the embryo between weeks 22 and 26 and cannot increase after birth, and that upper lids carry roughly 90 to 160 lashes.[6]

Length, thickness and darkness decline with age, plucked lashes take about seven to eight weeks to regrow, and constant pulling can cause permanent damage.[6] Lashes are not androgen-driven, so puberty does not change them.[6] These biological limits frame what any topical product could change: the visible look of existing hairs (coating, shine, hydration) versus the follicle count and cycle.

Latisse (bimatoprost), introduced by Allergan in the first quarter of 2009, was the first FDA-approved drug for eyelash growth; Wikipedia reports noticeable growth in about 16 weeks and up to a 25 percent increase in length, mainly on upper lashes.[6] Reported adverse effects of bimatoprost include eye redness, burning, darkening of the eyelid or skin beneath the eye, and permanent darkening of the iris, and the cosmetic formulation carries an infection risk if single-use applicators are reused.[8] Some cosmetic lash serums use peptides rather than prostaglandins because of regulations in Canada and California.[6]

Looksmax.org threads also discuss minoxidil on lashes and brows (including oral minoxidil), dermastamping, tinting and dye, and before-and-after posts of people reporting changes over a few months.[15][16][17][18][19] These are off-label or cosmetic approaches that members compare with oils, and they are not tested in the castor-oil literature.

Castor oil is generally described as low in toxicity when used topically. Wikipedia notes the seeds contain ricin, which is removed or deactivated in producing the oil, and an allergen that is absent from the oil.[2] Cold-pressed castor oil is considered non-toxic at normal doses.[13] Healthline reports allergic reactions are possible and that guidance advises patch testing, rinsing the eye with water if oil gets in, and checking that a product is pure castor oil rather than a blend.[4]

Eye-area conditions that can cause lash loss or irritation, such as blepharitis, trichiasis and Demodex mite infestation (found in the follicles of about 20 percent of people), are documented in Wikipedia's eyelash article, and people with eyelid symptoms are generally directed to eye-care professionals.[6]

Looksmax.org members discuss brows and lashes as part of the eye area, and threads range from lash lifts and tints to growth products.[10] In a thread asking whether castor oil for eyebrow growth is legitimate, one member answered yes and another said shaved brows return in two to four weeks, with tweezed ones taking longer.[5] A more recent thread on castor oil on brows and lashes continues the discussion, and other threads compare castor oil with minoxidil and other approaches.[12][15][16][20]

One user's thread asks which oil or serum is safest to grow lashes with and wants no irritation, reflecting the way the topic is framed: low-cost, low-risk first steps before prescription options.[10]

No studies found on castor oil for eyebrow or eyelash growth. A small 2021 randomized trial described by Healthline examined castor oil for blepharitis symptoms, not lash growth.[4] Related research on prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost, bimatoprost) shows lengthening and thickening of lashes, but those are different compounds.[7][8]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, castor oil is a common first suggestion for regrowing or thickening brows and lashes, usually alongside discussion of minoxidil, tinting and lash lifts.[5][12][15]

claims.claim: Castor oil regrows shaved or thinned brows.
Castor oil makes lashes look healthier even if not longer.
Ricinoleic acid blocks prostaglandin D2 and so grows hair.
Jamaican black castor oil works better than clear cold-pressed oil.
Minoxidil or prescription analogs work better than oils for lashes.
Down-turned or sparse lashes hurt how the eye area looks, so improving them helps canthal tilt.
